extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory and Aristotelian poetics; poets and critics studying poetic principles
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle’s criteria for what makes poetry (especially tragedy and epic) artistically true — e.g., rules about universals vs. particulars, probability/necessity, treatment of the marvellous, chance, and moral/causal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal (τὰ καθόλου) not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry's subject-matter is the universal (τὰ καθόλου) rather than the particular (τὰ καθ᾽ ὅκαστον); it abstracts from accidental details and thereby reveals permanent possibilities and the universal element in human nature and life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry 'liberates us from the tyranny of physical surroundings' and 'transforms facts into truths' — it should focus on enduring human possibilities rather than merely recounting individual occurrences (contrast with history).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet vs historian: relate what may happen, not what has happened
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential difference is that the poet relates what may happen (ἂν γένοιτο / δυνατά), whereas the historian relates what has happened; metre or prose does not determine the difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrative of real events might be in verse but remain history; poets must aim at plausibly possible actions rather than strict factual reportage (Herodotus example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and necessity as internal structural laws (κατὰ τὸ εἰκὸς ἢ τὸ ἀναγκαῖον)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem should exhibit a rigorous connexion of events where cause and event are linked in a sequence governed by probability or necessity — an inner law securing cohesion of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'probable' here governs internal coherence and the poem’s causal logic, not empirical frequency; the plot must maintain an unbroken chain of cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic 'probable' is not empirical average (εἰκός ≠ statistical likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The εἰκός of art is not determined by numerical averages of real life; characters in poetry are often exceptional, so their actions may be improbable in everyday life yet probable within the poem's logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge a character's plausibility by frequency in experience; judge by how convincingly actions follow from character and circumstance (e.g., heroes like Hamlet, Othello).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish errors of poetic art from errors of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor oversights, inconsistencies, or technical inaccuracies are not necessarily serious provided they leave the total impression unimpaired; errors affecting the essence of the poetic art are the real faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a factual mistake undermines the work's unity or causal logic; trivial technical mistakes can be tolerated if the artistic effect remains intact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Higher reality / idealization (βέλτιον, ὡς δεῖ): poetry may portray what 'ought to be'
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry can represent things that surpass empirical reality — 'not real but a higher reality' — showing what ought to be rather than what is; art reveals the immanent idea within particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Idealisation is legitimate when it reveals a truer, more intelligible form of things than raw empirical fact (examples: Sophocles' characters, Zeuxis' ideals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's licence to 'tell lies as he ought' (ψεῦδῆ λόγειν ὡς δεῖ) / primary fictional assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may make primary assumptions (an initial ψεῦδος) and create his own environment; starting from these poetic data he may proceed so long as the internal sequence and plausibility are preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic fiction succeeds by making the invented premises lead to events that would have occurred had the premises been facts; vivid detail and natural sequence help the audience accept the initial falsehood (Homeric example, the fallacy/paralogismos explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer 'probable impossibilities' to 'improbable possibilities'
rubrics_metrics.description: Art should render impossible things in a way that makes them seem probable; Aristotle prefers 'probable impossibilities' over 'improbable possibilities'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use artistic treatment to make remote or impossible events feel natural and inevitable; e.g., Homer's handling of marvels (Phaeacian ship, Odysseus' landing) or epic episodes that would be implausible on stage but work in narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational elements (ἄλογα) are more damaging than material impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are irrational (contradictory to the logical/moral order) provoke the intellect and are less admissible than mere material impossibilities, which art can render plausible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irrational incidents require strong justification and are more tolerable in epic than in drama; they must not break the causal/moral coherence of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional belief / δόξα can justify otherwise impossible elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Things enshrined in current tradition or popular belief (δόξα) — even if empirically false — may be proper material for poetry because they are 'so runs the tale' and have cultural coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an element is deeply rooted in the national mythology or collective imagination, a poet may incorporate it; such traditional marvellous elements may be integrated into a coherent poetic order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-sensitive admissibility: epic vs drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry may admit more marvellous, supernatural, or irrational elements than drama; drama is a typical representation of human action where motive and causal intelligibility are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In drama, irrational or motiveless actions are especially inadmissible and should be excluded or located outside the dramatic action; in epic, some license is permitted if the overall effect (wonder, admiration) is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral improbability (character inconsistency) is a grave defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Improbabilities that depend on character — actions that violate permanent facts of human nature or the motives proper to a situation — are particularly serious and artistic faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether actions follow from established character and motives; examples of unacceptable moral improbability include Oedipus' ignorance of Laius' death or implausible behaviour that betrays character logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist must purify and shape material (extract the ore from legend)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet's shaping activity is essential: he must free material from the accidental, trivial, and irrelevant, idealise legends and facts, and combine parts into a unified structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the poet's ability to select, refine, and unite traditional or historical material into a coherent, poetic whole rather than leaving it a loose chronicle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude chance / accident (τύχη) because it contradicts art's unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance and anomalous accidents (τύχη, τὸ αὐτόματον) are the antithesis of Art and introduce disorder; poetry should not rely on mere chance as a causal principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accidental or anomalous events are acceptable only if the poet can make them appear designed and part of the poem's internal logic; apologetic claims that something occurred by 'strange chance' are a misconception of fiction's principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even comedy should be framed on lines of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the connexion of incidents in comedy is looser than in tragedy, comedy’s incidents too should be 'framed on lines of probability' rather than being products of arbitrary chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not excuse comedic plot contrivances as mere accident; judge comedies by how plausibly incidents follow from character and situation, even if the rules of necessity are less strict than in tragedy.
